title: Christmas Cards to Strangers
text:
In the 1970s, the sociologist Phillip Kunz of Brigham Young University tried a simple experiment around the holidays. With his colleague Michael Woolcott, he picked names of families he had never met from a city directory and mailed each of them a Christmas card. There was no letter of explanation and no way for the recipients to know who he was.

Then the replies came in. A sizable share of the strangers sent a card back, some with family photos or long handwritten notes about their year. Hardly anyone asked who this person was or why he had written. Receiving a card seemed to call for sending one, and that was enough.

The researchers also varied how the cards were signed, to suggest a sender of higher or lower social status, and found that this affected how many people answered. The title of their paper, "Season's greetings: From my status to yours," reflected that interest. But what made the study famous was the basic result: people returned a greeting to a total stranger almost by reflex, because a gift received feels like a gift owed.
lesson: Reciprocity runs deep and fast. A small, sincere gesture toward someone is often returned, which makes it one of the simplest ways to open or renew a connection.
location: Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
source: Kunz, P. R., and Woolcott, M. (1976). Season's greetings: From my status to yours. Social Science Research, 5(3), 269-278.
caveat: The exact response figures are reported differently in popular retellings, so they are left out here.
